title: Design a Library Management System: Book, Member, Librarian, BookItem (copy), Reservation, Fine, search by title/author/ISBN, issue/return/renew.
topicTitle: LLD Problems: Parking Lot, Elevator, Chess, etc.
keyPoints: The critical modelling decision is separating Book (abstract title with ISBN, author) from BookItem (physical copy with barcode and status).
A Book has many BookItems in a one-to-many composition; lending operates on specific copies, not abstract titles.
Issue finds a free BookItem, marks it ISSUED with a due date; return marks it AVAILABLE and charges a fine if overdue.
Renewal extends the due date only when no other member has reserved the title.
Fine calculation is pulled into a FinePolicy interface so the library can switch between flat and tiered fines without touching lending logic.
Reservations notify the first waiting member when a copy returns, using an observer-style queue.
Concurrency requires per-title locking so the same copy is never issued to two members simultaneously.

s1_definition.oneliner: A library lends concrete copies of abstract titles, tracking issue, return, renewal, reservation, and fines.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Book** – the abstract title with ISBN, author, and name. Represents the concept, not a physical copy.
- **BookItem** – a physical copy with its own barcode, status (AVAILABLE, ISSUED, RESERVED), and due date.
- **Member** – a library member who can hold several issued items up to a configured limit.
- **Reservation** – a queue entry for a member waiting for a title whose copies are all out.
- **Fine** – computed by a `FinePolicy` when a book item is returned overdue.
- **LibrarianService** – orchestrates issue, return, renewal, and reservation operations.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of National Bank of India lending out physical gold certificates. The certificate design (Book) is one thing, but each printed copy (BookItem) is a separate physical object with its own barcode and status. Rajesh borrows a copy, Priya reserves one that is out, and if Rajesh returns late he pays a fine, exactly like a late fee on a loan repayment.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Book vs BookItem:
  ─────────────────

  Book (ISBN: 978-0134685991)
  │
  ├── BookItem (barcode: LIB-001, AVAILABLE)
  ├── BookItem (barcode: LIB-002, ISSUED to Rajesh)
  └── BookItem (barcode: LIB-003, RESERVED)
```

```text
  Issue Flow:
  ───────────

  Member requests ISBN
       │
       ▼
  Find free BookItem for that ISBN
       │
       ▼
  BookItem.issue(memberId, dueDate)
       │
       ▼
  Member.addIssuedItem(item)
       │
       ▼
  Return Ticket / Confirmation
```

```text
  Return Flow:
  ────────────

  Member returns BookItem
       │
       ▼
  Is overdue? ──yes──→ FinePolicy.computeFine(days)
       │                    │
       │ no                 ▼
       ▼              Charge fine
  BookItem.returnItem()
       │
       ▼
  Reservation? ──yes──→ Notify next member
       │
       │ no
       ▼
  Item available for anyone
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
When you design a library management system, the single most important modelling decision is separating the Book from the BookItem. A Book is the abstract title with its ISBN, author, and name, while a BookItem is one physical copy with its own barcode, status, and due date. A book has many items, so when a member borrows, you are lending a specific copy, not the abstract title, and this separation is what makes multi-copy lending correct.

The main operations are issue, return, renewal, and reservation. Issuing finds an available copy, marks it issued with a due date, and adds it to the member's issued list. Returning frees the copy and charges a fine if overdue. Renewal extends the due date but only when no one has reserved the title. Reservations use an observer-style queue: when a copy returns, the first waiting member is notified.

Fine calculation is pulled into a fine-policy interface so the library can move from a flat per-day fine to a tiered one without touching the lending logic. This is the Open/Closed Principle and the Strategy pattern working together. Search is backed by indexes on title, author, and ISBN for fast lookups.

The concurrency concern is that two members acting on the same title at the same instant must be serialised, otherwise a single copy could be double-issued. Per-title locking solves this. In banking at National Bank of India, this is the same discipline applied to lending any limited physical asset: distinguish the design from the instance, track status transitions precisely, and charge late fees through a replaceable policy.

Remember one sentence: a library separates the abstract Book from the physical BookItem, lends specific copies with due dates, and charges fines through a pluggable policy.
